Scent brings the lover into the poem

The woman’s voice opens the book, and she speaks more than anyone in it. Verse 3 begins with scent. His oils are fragrant, and his name is like oil poured out. A good name spreads as perfume does. The comparison makes attraction felt through the senses. Read these images as poetic comparisons, not a list of objects owned by the lovers. Ancient perfume vessels help make that sensory world concrete.

The lover’s invitation rests on the season. Verse 11 says the winter and the rain are over. Verses 12–13 add flowers, birdsong, figs, and blossoming vines. Everything is ready, so he says, “Arise.” Verse 7 warned not to wake love until it pleases. The two fit together. Love has a right time, as the spring does.

The phrase “him whom my soul loves” comes four times in verses 1–4. The word “sought” comes four times as well. The scene begins on her bed at night, so it may be a dream. In verse 2 she acts: she gets up and goes through the city. She searches in public and asks the guards. Verse 4 ends with finding and holding. The royal carriage in verses 7–8 needs sixty swords against the night.
The garden describes desire through a place

Verse 12 calls the woman a locked garden and a sealed fountain. The garden is hers, and it is not open to the public. Verses 13–14 fill it with rare spices and fruit. The picture is of great worth kept private. Verse 16 gives the key to her. She calls the winds and invites him in. “My garden” becomes “his garden” by her own word.
A missed opening changes the scene

In verse 3 the woman gives small reasons for not getting up. By verse 6 she has opened the door, and he has left. The moment was missed. Her search repeats chapter 3 with a different result. There the watchmen let her pass (3:3). Here they strike and wound her (verse 7). The poem lets love include bad timing and hurt.
Belonging follows a question about absence

In 2:16 the woman said, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” Verse 3 reverses the order. Now she says first, “I am my beloved’s.” This comes after the lost night of chapter 5. She states their belonging again and names where he is (verse 2). Verses 8–9 set her apart from a king’s many wives. Verse 9 calls her “unique.”
Praise leads into the woman’s invitation

Verse 10 gives a third form of the belonging line. She is his, and “his desire is toward me.” Genesis 3:16 used “desire” in a sentence about strain between husband and wife. Here the desire is mutual and glad. In verses 11–12 she makes the plan. She says, “Let’s go,” “let’s lodge,” and “let’s see.” The praise she has received leads to her own invitation.
The ending places love beyond purchase

Verses 6–7 are the one place this book speaks about love in general. Many waters cannot put it out. A man who offered all his wealth for it would be scorned. Love cannot be drowned, and it cannot be bought. Two scenes then test that claim. Her brothers plan to guard her, and she says she guards herself (verses 8–10). Solomon’s vineyard earns silver, and hers is not for rent (verses 11–12).
